Getting started with optimix

Source: vignettes/optimix.Rmd
optimix.Rmd
library(optimix)

Why

An agronomist has written a cost function over two decision variables – say a nitrogen rate and a sowing density – and wants the combination that minimises it under a fixed number of trial runs. She does not know, before she starts, whether that cost surface is a smooth bowl, has a ripple hiding a second dip, or is something else entirely, and she does not want to choose a different optimisation package for every shape she might meet. optimix is built for exactly that: one call that takes a function and a box, and returns the best point it can find within the budget, whatever the surface turns out to be. This vignette walks the whole surface of the package – both front doors, the result it hands back, and what the optimiser actually found – and closes by showing that optimum sitting inside the landscape it was found in.

What

optimix() is the single verb: it takes an objective function (or an optim_problem()) and a design space, chooses or uses a named optimiser, and returns an optimix_result. optim_problem() is the typed contract behind it – fn, space (typically a space_box()), an optional evaluation budget, warm start and seed – and is what the easy path builds internally from fn, lower and upper. list_optimisers() reports the registry of engines optimix knows about, which of their backend packages are installed, and the traits (global, noise_tolerant, emits_map) the selector reads. The result behaves like a stats::optim() return value, with coef(), as.data.frame() and as_optim() as read-outs for code that expects exactly that shape.

Do

The easy path

The easy path takes a function and box bounds, in the spirit of stats::optim(). The objective below is a synthetic quadratic bowl centred on the origin, and method = "base_optim" names the zero-dependency core engine directly, so this chunk needs nothing beyond base R:

result <- optimix(
  function(x) sum(x^2),
  lower = c(-5, -5),
  upper = c(5, 5),
  method = "base_optim"
)
result
#> <optimix_result>
#>   optimiser : base_optim
#>   value     : 0
#>   par       : 0, 0
#>   evals     : 5
#>   converged : yes

minimise() and maximise() are readable aliases for the same call.

Which optimisers are available

With the default method = "auto", optimix selects an optimiser for the problem from those whose package is installed, and records the choice in the result’s provenance. list_optimisers() shows what is available on this build:

lo <- list_optimisers()
lo
#>              name     package installed global noise_tolerant emits_map
#> 1      base_optim        base      TRUE  FALSE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 2        bayesopt DiceKriging      TRUE   TRUE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 3           cmaes       cmaes      TRUE   TRUE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 4         deoptim     DEoptim      TRUE   TRUE           TRUE     FALSE
#> 5        deoptimr    DEoptimR      TRUE   TRUE           TRUE     FALSE
#> 6    dfoptim_hjkb     dfoptim      TRUE  FALSE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 7           gensa       GenSA      TRUE   TRUE           TRUE     FALSE
#> 8   nloptr_bobyqa      nloptr      TRUE  FALSE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 9  nloptr_directl      nloptr      TRUE   TRUE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 10        perm_sa        base      TRUE   TRUE          FALSE     FALSE
#> 11   proxymix_map    proxymix      TRUE   TRUE          FALSE      TRUE

An optim()-compatible result

The result is shaped like a stats::optim() return value – par, value, counts, convergence, message – so existing code keeps working, with optimix extras alongside. The usual accessors apply:

coef(result)
#> [1] 0 0
as.data.frame(result)
#>   x1 x2 value  optimiser
#> 1  0  0     0 base_optim
as_optim(result)
#> $par
#> [1] 0 0
#> 
#> $value
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $counts
#> function gradient 
#>        5       NA 
#> 
#> $convergence
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $message
#> [1] "CONVERGENCE: NORM OF PROJECTED GRADIENT <= PGTOL"

The power path

For noise, an evaluation budget, a warm start, or a seed, build an optim_problem() directly and pass it to optimix(). The objective below is a synthetic bowl shifted to (1, 1), capped at 2000 evaluations:

problem <- optim_problem(
  fn = function(x) sum((x - 1)^2),
  space = space_box(lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5)),
  max_evals = 2000
)
power_result <- optimix(problem, method = "base_optim")
power_result
#> <optimix_result>
#>   optimiser : base_optim
#>   value     : 0
#>   par       : 1, 1
#>   evals     : 20
#>   converged : yes

The same problem object is what the easy path builds behind the scenes – one contract, two front doors.

A figure: where the optimum sits in the landscape

None of the results above shows what the objective actually looks like around the point that was returned. The synthetic surface below is a bowl centred near (2, -1.5) with a small sinusoidal ripple layered on top, so it is not quite the clean quadratic of the two examples above; method = "auto" is left to choose the engine, exactly as a first-time user would call it:

set.seed(9)
rippled_bowl <- function(x) {
  sum((x - c(2, -1.5))^2) + 0.4 * sin(3 * x[1]) * cos(2 * x[2])
}
auto_result <- optimix(
  rippled_bowl, lower = c(-5, -5), upper = c(5, 5), method = "auto"
)
auto_result
#> <optimix_result>
#>   optimiser : nloptr_bobyqa
#>   value     : -0.156071
#>   par       :  2.3848, -1.5269
#>   evals     : 313
#>   converged : yes
auto_result$provenance$engine
#> [1] "nloptr_bobyqa"
gx <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 100L)
gy <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 100L)
grid_df <- expand.grid(x1 = gx, x2 = gy)
grid_df$z <- apply(
  grid_df, 1L, function(row) rippled_bowl(c(row[["x1"]], row[["x2"]]))
)
opt_df <- data.frame(x1 = auto_result$par[1L], x2 = auto_result$par[2L])
ggplot2::ggplot(grid_df, ggplot2::aes(x1, x2, z = z)) +
  ggplot2::geom_contour_filled(bins = 12L) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "cost", guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = opt_df, ggplot2::aes(x1, x2), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "white", fill = "firebrick", shape = 21L, size = 3L, stroke = 1L
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "x1 (nitrogen-rate-style decision variable)",
    y = "x2 (sowing-density-style decision variable)",
    title = "Where the returned optimum sits in the full landscape"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

The rippled synthetic bowl over its full search box, with the optimum optimix found marked in red. The ripple bends the contours away from a perfect ellipse without moving the deepest point far from the unperturbed bowl’s centre.

Read

The easy-path bowl is solved exactly: optimix() returns a value of 0 at par = (0, 0), using 5 evaluations of the zero-dependency base_optim engine. The registry carries 11 named optimisers, of which 11 are installed and available on this build – every engine behind a Suggests package plus the base engine and the permutation annealer, since every optional package checked in the DESCRIPTION happens to be present here. The accessors read the same result three ways: coef() returns the bare parameter vector, as.data.frame() adds the objective value and the engine name as columns, and as_optim() strips the result back down to the five components a stats::optim()-based caller expects. The power-path bowl, shifted to (1, 1), is also solved exactly, in 20 evaluations against its 2000-call budget – the budget is a ceiling the engine did not need to spend.

The rippled bowl is where a single number stops being enough. method = "auto" chose nloptr_bobyqa for it, reaching a value of -0.1561 at par = (2.385, -1.527). Read on its own, that pair of numbers says nothing about how close the ripple came to hiding a second, competing dip nearby, or how far the optimum sits from the edges of the search box. The figure answers both at a glance: the returned point sits inside the deepest contour band, close to the unperturbed bowl’s centre at (2, -1.5), and the ripple bends the bands without creating a second dark region the optimum could have missed.

Limits

This vignette runs one call per example and reads its result in isolation; it does not compare engines against each other, examine why method = "auto" chose one engine over another, or characterise a budget’s effect on solution quality – The auto selector and racing does both. It also stays in two dimensions, in a continuous box, with a single global optimum in each example: optimix_map() for a surface with several equally good optima, and space_permutation() for search over orderings rather than real-valued points, are both left to their own vignettes. Nothing here demonstrates that a chosen engine failed to converge, or shows the classed abstention a caller can check for when it did; that machinery is exercised directly in Mapping optima and the orchestra manifest.

What to read next

The auto selector and racing explains the rules and the race behind method = "auto", states the held-out evidence for when it wins, and introduces the provenance fields this vignette only prints in passing. Mapping optima and the orchestra manifest answers “what if there is more than one good answer”, and shows the typed abstention a caller receives when a request cannot be honoured. Combinatorial optimisation and delta evaluation moves from real-valued boxes to orderings, for scheduling- and assignment-shaped problems.

Reproduce

Seed 9 for the rippled-bowl figure; the two quadratic-bowl examples are deterministic and draw no random numbers.
